title: Autonomous completion of whole operations at expert level

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a surgical system that can perceive the operative field, decide what to do next, and carry out complete soft-tissue operations with outcomes matching expert surgeons, without a person continuously directing instrument motion. Its scope includes exposure, dissection, resection or repair, control of bleeding, and closure wherever those phases are required. Demonstrating the capability across more than one procedure class is part of the concept: completing a single suturing task or one phase of an operation would establish a narrower capability.

Conceptual distinction: autonomy concerns who makes and executes operative decisions, rather than the robot’s appearance or the surgeon’s location. A remotely controlled robot can perform surgery while a human still supplies the decisions and instrument commands. The July 2026 humanoid surgical demonstration illustrates this distinction: the supplied review identifies it as teleoperation. The proposed innovation could still include human supervision, approval of plans, and emergency takeover; it does not require error-free performance or the removal of all human responsibility.

significance.text: Conditional significance: expert-level whole-operation autonomy would reduce the need for an expert surgeon to continuously translate judgments into instrument movements throughout each validated operation. It would make an integrated repertoire of surgical perception, decisions, and actions reproducible through a technical system. That would be a major change in how operative expertise is delivered, even if a qualified team remained responsible for patient selection, supervision, rescue, and postoperative care.

Potential benefits require separate demonstrations. Matching expert surgeons on average safety and efficacy would not by itself show reduced variability between cases, institutions, or operators. More consistent execution is an intended benefit that would need direct measurement. Wider access outside specialist centers is a conditional downstream possibility, dependent on affordable deployment, maintenance, infrastructure, trained support teams, and timely rescue when the system encounters a problem it cannot handle.

The analogy to turning a manual craft into a reproducible technology has limits. Surgical outcomes also depend on disease, anatomy, patient physiology, treatment selection, and care before and after the operation. Autonomy over a validated repertoire would not establish competence in every operation a human surgeon can perform, nor would remote operation alone establish autonomy. The documented 2026 porcine work supports the feasibility of a surgeon-controlled robotic platform, not the broader substitution of autonomous judgment for continuous human control.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability sought is reliable integration of all required operative phases across distinct operations, with both autonomous completion and expert-level clinical outcomes. This is a larger engineering objective than executing a bounded maneuver: the system must maintain an understanding of the patient and operative field, choose and revise a plan, recognize when a phase is complete, and manage the consequences of its actions throughout the operation. The supplied evidence does not establish whether this broader capability remains unmet worldwide as of November 1, 2026; it establishes neither its achievement nor a comprehensive search for its absence.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include tracking deforming tissue, recognizing anatomy and safe dissection planes under changing visibility, controlling force without damaging tissue, and coordinating exposure with cutting, repair, and hemostasis. Bleeding and obscured planes are useful descriptions of the target problem, but the readable evidence retained in this packet does not independently substantiate those particular assertions. They are presented here as challenges the proposed system would need to address, rather than as verified findings from the cited demonstrations.

Engineering synthesis: an integrated system also needs dependable detection of uncertainty, injury, incomplete treatment, and departures from the planned anatomy or workflow. It must recover safely when possible and request human assistance early enough when recovery exceeds its competence. The central difficulty is maintaining these abilities through interacting phases and unfamiliar variations, while defining a practical boundary beyond which autonomous operation should stop. The available teleoperation evidence does not demonstrate that autonomous decision-making and recovery capability.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes a January 26, 2022 Science Robotics study in which the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot, STAR, performed laparoscopic small-bowel anastomosis in porcine models followed over a one-week survival period. It reports that an operator selected among robot-generated plans and that phantom experiments showed greater consistency than manual laparoscopy and surgeon-operated robotic suturing. The accompanying Johns Hopkins account reportedly describes four animals and minimal human intervention. These details are retained as attributed research reports: the source index contains no captured text for either source, so the validated review could not verify the sample size, survival, comparisons, or exact intervention burden. Even if confirmed, anastomosis is a bounded component of surgery and would not establish the proposed breadth of complete operations.

The supplied research also reports that the July 9, 2025 Science Robotics paper on SRT-H, a hierarchical system using language-conditioned imitation learning, achieved 100% success across eight ex vivo porcine gallbladders without human intervention during the clipping-and-cutting phase of cholecystectomy. That percentage concerns the reported eight-specimen experiment and its defined phase, not clinical reliability or complete-operation success. The research attributes to December 1, 2025 author correspondence a clarification that the work concerned a phase of cholecystectomy in pig cadavers, with in vivo and human studies still ahead. Neither the paper nor that correspondence has captured source text in this packet, so these numerical results and qualifications could not be independently verified by the supplied review. The research identifies a journal publication and an earlier manuscript version; the missing evidence does not justify treating the result as false or as merely an unpublished preprint.

The strongest retained evidence concerns the Nature paper published July 8, 2026, which describes a humanoid laparoscopic teleoperation framework evaluated through benchtop testing, dry-laboratory user studies, and in vivo porcine studies. Its subscription preview includes a textual figure listing identifying live porcine laparoscopic cholecystectomies. A July 31 Nature Medicine research highlight states that a human surgeon controlled the robot remotely, and the associated author responses to peer review also confirm teleoperation. These materials support a dated demonstration of surgeon-controlled robotic surgery in living pigs; they do not demonstrate autonomous completion or expert-level human clinical outcomes.

Access limits constrain interpretation of the 2026 work. The retained Nature article is a subscription preview rather than an available full article body, and the research highlight is also partial. The review had a textual figure listing, not an independent inspection of the figure or operative outcomes. The peer-review correspondence has gaps in extracted text and is not the final methods section. Another supplementary PDF yielded essentially no usable text, and a purported paper download instead contained an unrelated 2020 internship report. Those files add no verified operative results and do not contradict the usable teleoperation evidence.

The packet does not establish the current status of all commercial surgical or telesurgery platforms, including the candidate’s broad statement about da Vinci and other systems. It also supplies no bounded search record supporting the assertion that no human trial of autonomous whole-operation completion had been identified by November 1, 2026. The appropriate conclusion is limited: the retained readable evidence demonstrates teleoperated porcine surgery, while the earlier autonomous milestones remain attributed reports and the present worldwide frontier cannot be determined from this packet.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: evaluate the system prospectively in living humans on two anatomically different complete operations, against expert surgeons working in the same institutions. Prespecify the full set of operative phases and require completion without continuous manual control of instrument trajectories. Define procedure-specific safety and efficacy endpoints, clinically justified non-inferiority margins, adequate sample sizes, eligibility criteria, and the permitted forms of human supervision or assistance. Thirty-day outcomes would be an initial benchmark, with longer follow-up wherever needed to assess durability of repair or treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard

completion_criteria.text: Clinical outcomes and autonomous completion should be separate endpoints. The protocol should define when a human must take over, distinguish plan approval from manual instrument control, and report every assistance event and takeover with its reason and timing. Takeovers should be counted under a prespecified autonomy-success endpoint so that successful expert rescue cannot be mistaken for autonomous completion. Patient safety can be preserved through rescue while the attempted autonomous operation still fails its completion criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical outcomes and autonomous completion should be separate

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: repeat the demonstration across institutions, support teams, and representative eligible patients, reporting outcomes by operation and relevant anatomical or clinical variation. State exclusions, equipment and infrastructure needs, rescue arrangements, and the circumstances in which the system declines or stops an operation. Measure variability separately if improved consistency is claimed. Success on intestinal suturing alone or one ex vivo gallbladder phase would not meet this scope; success on two complete operations would demonstrate breadth within tested conditions, not universal surgical competence.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SUR-11, “Real-time cellular and molecular vision of the intact operative field,” could provide richer information for identifying tissue and treatment boundaries. SUR-06 concerns the decisions and actions that use operative information; improved vision alone does not establish autonomous completion, and this concept does not require achievement of every capability envisioned by SUR-11.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-07, “Incisionless resection and reconstruction inside the closed body,” changes access and operative delivery, whereas SUR-06 changes who controls execution. Either could be developed without the other. SUR-10, “Cell-identity-selective extirpation inside an organ that keeps working,” changes the biological selectivity of tissue removal; autonomy might deliver that treatment, but ordinary expert-level autonomous resection would not establish cell-selective extirpation.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-01, “Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive,” addresses immune acceptance; SUR-02, “Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation,” addresses durable use of animal organs; SUR-03, “Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs,” addresses organ preservation; and SUR-12, “Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation,” addresses organ manufacture. Autonomous surgery could assist implantation or associated procedures, but cannot by itself solve tolerance, xenograft durability, cryopreservation, or organ construction.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-04, “Restoration of volitional function after complete spinal cord transection,” targets neurological recovery, and SUR-05, “Adult surgical wounds that heal by regeneration rather than fibrosis,” targets the biological response to injury. SUR-09, “Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply,” targets construction of replacement tissues. An autonomous system might perform interventions associated with these capabilities, but accurate operative execution does not establish neural reconnection, regenerative healing, or a viable replacement part.

Roster-based synthesis: SUR-08, “Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest,” concerns creating a recoverable physiological state that permits treatment after otherwise catastrophic blood loss. SUR-06 concerns performing the treatment itself. Autonomous control of hemorrhage could become complementary, but neither metabolic arrest nor autonomous operative execution establishes the other capability.

change_log.change: Preserved SUR-06’s identity and whole-operation, multiple-procedure scope while separating the target capability from claims that it remains globally unachieved.
change_log.reason: The review supports retaining the concept but supplies no bounded contemporary search establishing its absence.

change_log.change: Retained the 2022 STAR and 2025 SRT-H dates, quantitative reports, experimental settings, and intervention qualifications as explicitly attributed research accounts.
change_log.reason: Their source texts were not captured for review. Preserving qualified detail integrates the research without treating unverified reports as established findings or false results.

change_log.change: Clarified that the reported eight-specimen, 100% SRT-H result concerns an ex vivo operative phase.
change_log.reason: Phase-level success does not establish complete cholecystectomy, living-animal performance, human efficacy, or general clinical reliability.

change_log.change: Identified the July 2026 humanoid work as teleoperation and corrected the account of source access to a subscription preview with partial supporting materials.
change_log.reason: The preview, research highlight, and extracted author correspondence support human control; they do not provide complete methods or independently inspectable operative outcomes.

change_log.change: Removed categorical assertions about all commercial platforms and the absence of human autonomy trials.
change_log.reason: The packet does not verify those broad claims or document a search sufficient to establish them.

change_log.change: Made improved consistency and broader access conditional, and retained limits on universal competence and supervision.
change_log.reason: Expert-level non-inferiority does not demonstrate reduced variability, and deployment benefits depend on resources, support, and rescue capacity.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed evaluation with separate autonomy and clinical endpoints, takeover accounting, justified margins, adequate samples, reproducibility, and procedure-appropriate follow-up.
change_log.reason: Expert rescue can preserve clinical outcomes without demonstrating autonomous completion, and 30-day outcomes may not capture treatment durability.

change_log.change: Added concrete engineering barriers as labeled synthesis and distinguished SUR-06 from every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: The record needs to explain the integration challenge and relevant overlaps without presenting inferred barriers as verified study findings or merging distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: The 2022 STAR paper and Johns Hopkins report need readable source evidence to verify the four-animal account, one-week survival, phantom comparisons, plan selection, and exact human intervention burden.

The 2025 SRT-H paper and reported December correspondence need readable evidence to verify the eight-specimen success result, task boundaries, intervention accounting, and stated path toward in vivo and human work.
The worldwide status of autonomous whole-operation surgery as of November 1, 2026 remains undetermined because no bounded search record was supplied.
The status of individual commercial surgical platforms and any relevant human autonomy trials is not established by this packet.

Full methods and operative outcomes for the July 2026 humanoid study cannot be reconstructed from the preview, partial highlight, and incompletely extracted correspondence. The blank supplementary extraction provides no additional usable evidence.
The engineering discussion of bleeding, obscured planes, force control, and recovery is retained as conceptual synthesis; the supplied readable sources do not directly verify all of these barriers.
The proposed evaluation still requires selection of operations, eligibility boundaries, endpoint definitions, non-inferiority margins, sample sizes, assistance rules, and follow-up durations.

The review’s recommendation to replace the earlier autonomous milestone accounts solely with a missing-evidence statement was not adopted in full: their useful details are retained with explicit attribution and verification limits, as required to preserve uncertain research without overstating it.
